title: One address, from TLB hit to page fault

steps.say: The program loads virtual address 0x7F3A2010. That is page 0x7F3A2, offset 0x010. The CPU must turn it into a real RAM address.
The TLB (a small cache of translations) does not have page 0x7F3A2. This is a TLB miss.
The hardware walks the page table: 4 reads from RAM, about 20 ns each when cached, up to 100+ ns when not.
The entry says: present, frame 0x1A2B. The translation goes into the TLB so the next access is fast.
Now the real address is 0x1A2B010. One RAM read costs about 80 ns.
The next access to the same page is a TLB hit: about 1 ns for the translation. This is why locality matters.
Now the program touches page 0x7F3A9. Its entry is marked not present. The CPU raises a page fault and the OS takes over.
The OS finds the data in swap and reads one 4 KB page from the SSD. This takes about 100 microseconds, roughly 1,000 times slower than RAM.
The OS writes the new entry (frame 0x3C4D, present) and restarts the instruction. On a hard disk this fault would take about 10 ms.
Summary of costs: TLB hit ~1 ns, TLB miss ~100 ns, page fault from SSD ~100,000 ns.

title: A read, a hit, and a dirty write

steps.say: The app reads 4 KB at file offset 8192. That is file page 2. The kernel first looks in the page cache.
Page 2 is not in the cache: a miss. The kernel must go to the SSD.
The SSD read takes about 100 microseconds. The kernel notices a sequential pattern and also reads pages 3 and 4 ahead of time (readahead).
Page 2 is now in RAM and is copied to the app. The cache keeps it.
Reading page 2 again is a hit. No disk, about 1 microsecond for the syscall and copy: around 100 times faster.
Now the app writes 100 bytes into page 2. The kernel changes the cached copy only and marks the page dirty. write() returns in about 2 microseconds.
A background thread writes dirty pages back after about 30 seconds. Until then the new data exists only in RAM.
Failure case: power is lost at second 20. The write is gone, even though write() said success. The app should have called fsync.
fsync() forces the write to the SSD now. It costs about 0.1 to 2 ms, so databases batch it. After it, page 2 is clean and safe.

title: mmap: pages load only when touched

steps.say: mmap() maps the 1 GB file at 0x7F00_0000. The call is fast: it only records a range. No file data is read yet.
The program reads address 0x7F00_5000, which is file page 5. There is no page table entry, so the CPU raises a page fault.
The kernel looks in the page cache. Page 5 is not there. This is a major fault, because disk is needed.
It reads 4 KB from the file. About 100 microseconds on an SSD.
The kernel fills the page table entry to point at that frame and restarts the load. The program never called read().
Touching page 5 again costs only a normal memory access, about 80 ns, with no system call. This is why mmap can beat read().
A second process maps the same file. It points at the same cached frame, so no extra RAM is used: sharing for free.
A write to a MAP_SHARED page marks it dirty. The kernel writes it back later, or when you call msync.
Failure case: another program truncates the file to 4 KB. The next access to page 5 has no data behind it, so the process gets SIGBUS and dies.

title: Fair scheduling: smallest runtime goes first

steps.say: Three tasks want the CPU. Each has a virtual runtime (vrt): how much CPU time it already got. The scheduler always picks the smallest.
A has the smallest vrt (10.0 ms), so A runs. The time slice is about 4 ms.
After 4 ms, A's vrt is 14.0. B is now the smallest, so the scheduler switches to B. Everyone gets a fair share.
Task D finishes disk I/O and wakes up. It slept, so its vrt is low (10.5). It runs next: interactive tasks get fast response.
C is a CPU hog, so its vrt is highest (12.0). It waits its turn, but never starves: its vrt does not grow while it waits.
Priorities work through weights. A nice-0 task has weight 1024, a nice-10 task about 110. So nice-10 gets roughly 10 times less CPU.
Failure case: 100 runnable tasks on one core. The target latency is about 6 ms, but each task needs a minimum slice of 0.75 ms.
So each task waits about 100 x 0.75 = 75 ms for its turn. This is why an overloaded server feels slow even if no single task is bad.

title: What a context switch really costs

steps.say: Process A has used its 4 ms slice. A timer interrupt fires at 1000 Hz.
The CPU jumps into the kernel (mode switch, about 100 ns). The scheduler picks Process B.
The kernel saves A's registers: 16 general registers, instruction pointer 0x401A2C, stack pointer, flags. About 0.5 microseconds.
It switches to B's page table by writing the CR3 register. Without tagged TLB entries, the whole TLB is flushed.
It loads B's saved registers and returns to user mode. The direct cost is about 1 to 2 microseconds.
The hidden cost is bigger. B starts with a cold TLB and cold caches: each miss costs 100 ns instead of 1 ns.
B may need to refill hundreds of cache lines and TLB entries, so the real cost is often 10 to 50 microseconds.
Failure case: 10,000 switches per second at 30 us each means 30 percent of one core is wasted. Fewer threads and longer slices reduce this.

title: A lost update, a lock, and contention

steps.say: No lock yet. Both threads run counter++ at the same time. The value in memory is 41.
Both threads read 41 into a register, before either writes back.
Each thread adds 1 and writes 42. Two increments happened, but the counter is 42, not 43. One update is lost: a data race.
Fix: protect the update with a lock. Thread 1 takes it with one atomic compare-and-swap (CAS), about 20 ns when nobody else wants it.
Thread 2 tries the lock, the CAS fails. It spins a few times (burning CPU), then asks the kernel to put it to sleep with a futex call.
Thread 1 does its update inside the lock: 41 becomes 42. Thread 2 is waiting and doing nothing useful.
Thread 1 unlocks and wakes Thread 2. The wake-up goes through the scheduler and takes about 5 to 50 microseconds, 250 to 2,500 times the 20 ns fast path.
Thread 2 takes the lock and writes 43. The answer is correct now.
Cost case: with 32 threads on one hot lock, 31 are always asleep. Throughput can be lower than with 1 thread. Keep critical sections short and split locks.

title: Two threads wait for each other forever

steps.say: Two threads, two locks. Thread 1 will lock A then B. Thread 2 will lock B then A. The order is different.
Thread 1 takes Lock A. It works for about 1 ms.
At the same time, Thread 2 takes Lock B.
Thread 1 now asks for Lock B. It is held by Thread 2, so Thread 1 waits.
Thread 2 asks for Lock A. It is held by Thread 1, so Thread 2 waits too.
There is a cycle: T1 holds A and wants B; T2 holds B and wants A. Nobody can move. CPU use drops to 0 percent and requests hang.
The four conditions for deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one and it cannot happen.
Best fix: a global lock order. Everyone must take A before B. Thread 2 now asks for A first and waits with nothing held.
Thread 1 now gets Lock B too, because Thread 2 holds nothing.
Thread 1 finishes and releases both locks. Then Thread 2 runs: A, then B. No cycle is possible. Other fixes: try-lock with a timeout, or one big lock.

title: Condition variable: wait in a while loop

steps.say: The queue is empty. Consumer 1 takes the mutex and checks the queue. 0 items, so it must wait.
cond_wait does two things atomically: it releases the mutex and puts C1 to sleep. If these were separate, a signal could slip in between and be lost.
Consumer 1 sleeps and uses no CPU: no busy-waiting. Consumer 2 is busy with other work and is not waiting.
The producer locks the mutex, pushes one item and unlocks. The queue now has 1 item.
It calls signal. The kernel wakes Consumer 1. This costs a few microseconds, but C1 is still not running yet.
Before C1 gets the mutex back, Consumer 2 finishes its work, locks the mutex, and takes the item. The queue is empty again.
Now C1 gets the mutex. If the code was `if (empty) wait;` it would go on and pop from an empty queue: a crash or garbage. This is a stolen or spurious wakeup.
Correct code: `while (empty) wait;`. C1 re-checks the queue, sees 0 items, and goes back to sleep. Always test the condition in a loop.

title: malloc, free and fragmentation

steps.say: The heap is cut into 64-byte chunks starting at 0x1000. All 8 chunks, A to H, are in use. Each box shows its address.
The program frees A, C, E and G. A free is fast: about 20 ns, it just puts the chunk on a free list.
Total free memory is 4 x 64 = 256 bytes. That looks like plenty.
Now the program asks for malloc(128). That needs two free chunks side by side. Every free chunk has a used neighbour.
The request fails although 256 bytes are free. This is external fragmentation: memory is free but cut into pieces that are too small.
The allocator must ask the kernel for more memory with brk or mmap. This costs about 1 to 5 microseconds, plus page faults when new pages are first touched.
A better outcome: the program frees B. Now A, B and C are neighbours and all free.
The allocator coalesces A, B and C into one 192-byte block. malloc(128) now fits with no kernel call, in about 20 ns.

title: Mark and sweep, and the pause

steps.say: The heap holds five objects. Roots (stack variables and globals) point to A. A points to B, B points to E. C and D point to each other.
The program keeps allocating. The heap is 95 percent full (about 1.9 GB of 2 GB), so a collection starts.
Stop the world: all application threads pause, so the object graph cannot change while GC looks at it.
Mark phase: start at the roots. Visit A and mark it live.
Follow A's pointer to B, then B's pointer to E. All three are live.
C and D were never reached. They point to each other, but no root leads to them. A cycle does not keep an object alive here.
Sweep phase: free every unmarked object. C and D go back to the free space.
The application resumes. For a 2 GB heap with a small live set the pause was about 12 ms. Cost grows with the amount of live data.
Failure case: with 20 GB of live data a full stop-the-world pause can last seconds. Requests time out. Generational and concurrent collectors cut this to under 1 to 10 ms.

title: One miss loads 64 bytes

steps.say: The program sums int a[1000] in order. The array starts at 0x1000. Each int is 4 bytes. First read: a[0] at 0x1000.
L1 miss (checked in 4 cycles). L2 and L3 miss too (about 40 cycles). The request goes to RAM.
RAM answers in about 200 cycles (70 ns at 3 GHz). It does not send 4 bytes, it sends the whole 64-byte line 0x1000 to 0x103F.
a[1] to a[15] are in the same line. Each is an L1 hit: 4 cycles (about 1 ns). One miss paid for 16 reads.
Average cost: (200 + 15 x 4) / 16 = 16 cycles per int. The hardware prefetcher also fetches the next line early, so it is often even less.
Now the bad case: read every 16th int (stride 64 bytes): a[0], a[16], a[32]. Each read touches a new line.
Every read is a full miss: 200 cycles each. That is 12 times slower per access (200 vs 16). Same data size, very different speed.
Walking a 2D array by column is this worst case. A 4096-int-wide matrix has a stride of 16 KB, and the lines can also fight for the same cache sets, which makes it worse.
Rule: walk memory in order and keep related fields together. Use all 64 bytes of each line you pay for.

title: MESI states and false sharing

steps.say: One 64-byte cache line at 0x2000 holds two variables: x (offset 0) and y (offset 8). They are separate, but share one line.
Core 0 reads x. It is the only core with the line, so the state is E (Exclusive). A read costs one fetch, about 40 cycles from L3.
Core 1 reads y. The line is copied to Core 1. Now both cores have it, both in state S (Shared).
Core 0 writes x. To write, it needs the line alone. It sends an invalidate to Core 1, whose copy becomes I (Invalid). Core 0 becomes M (Modified).
Core 1 writes y. It has no valid copy, so it asks for the line. Core 0 must send its modified line (about 60 to 100 ns across cores) and drops to I.
Core 0 writes x again. The line moves back. The two cores keep stealing the line from each other.
This is false sharing: the threads share no data, but share a line. Each write costs about 80 ns instead of 1 ns. A loop of 100 million increments can take 8 s instead of 0.1 s.
Fix: pad or align each hot variable to its own 64-byte line, so that y moves to 0x2040.
Now each core keeps its own line in M state and writes at L1 speed, 1 ns per write, with no traffic between cores.

title: A 5-stage pipeline and a stall

steps.say: Cycle 1: instruction i1 enters Fetch (IF). The CPU has 5 stages. Each stage does one small job per cycle.
Cycle 2: i1 moves to Decode. At the same time, i2 is fetched. Stages work in parallel, like an assembly line.
Cycle 3: i1 executes, i2 decodes, i3 is fetched. Three instructions are in flight.
Cycle 4: four instructions in flight. Nothing is finished yet: this is the fill time of 4 cycles.
Cycle 5: i1 finishes (WB). But i3 needs r1, and i2 (a load) has not read memory yet. i3 must wait, so a bubble (an empty slot) goes into EX. This is a load-use stall.
Cycle 6: i2 finishes. i3 now gets r1 and executes. i4 was held back by the stall. 1 cycle lost.
Cycle 7: the bubble travels down the pipe doing nothing. i3 is in MEM, i4 in EX.
Cycle 8: i3 finishes. The bubble leaves the pipe.

Cycle 9: i4 finishes. 4 instructions took 9 cycles, 5 of them lost to filling and 1 stall. A long run reaches about 1 instruction per cycle. A mispredicted branch (see branch prediction) would flush all stages: 15 to 20 cycles.

title: Out-of-order execution hides a cache miss

steps.say: Five instructions are fetched into the reorder buffer (ROB). The CPU may run them in any order when their inputs are ready.
Instruction 1 loads from memory, and the data is not in any cache. It will take about 200 cycles.
Instruction 2 needs r1, so it must wait. An in-order CPU would stop here for 200 cycles and run nothing else.
Instructions 3 and 5 do not need r1. They run now, in the same cycle on different units. The CPU looks ahead past the stuck instruction.
Instruction 4 uses r3. When the multiply ends (3 cycles), 4 runs too. By cycle 5 everything except 1 and 2 is done.
Results wait in the ROB. They cannot retire yet: instructions must commit in program order, so the program looks sequential.
Cycle 200: the data arrives. Instruction 1 finishes, 2 runs in cycle 201, and all five retire together in a burst.
Failure case: the ROB holds 224 instructions, about 56 cycles of work at 4 per cycle. A 200-cycle miss still stalls the CPU once the ROB is full. Two misses in a row cost double.

title: Predict a branch, or flush the pipeline

steps.say: A loop tests each array item. The CPU can't wait ~15 cycles to learn the answer, so it guesses and keeps fetching.
Sorted array: the first 1,000 items are all >= 128, so the branch is taken every time. The 2-bit counter saturates at 11 (strongly taken).
Prediction is right again and again. Fetch runs ahead on the right path. Cost: 0 extra cycles, almost 100 percent correct.
Now a random array: half the items are < 128. The branch is taken, not taken, taken, not taken...
Predictor says taken, and Fetch loads ~20 instructions from that path. They are in the pipeline when the branch executes.
Execute finds the item was 90: NOT taken. The prediction was wrong.
The CPU flushes all wrong-path work and restarts fetching at the right address. This costs about 15 to 20 cycles, around 5 ns at 4 GHz.
Cost with random data: 1 million items x 50 percent wrong x 17 cycles = 8.5 million cycles, about 2 ms at 4 GHz. The sorted array pays almost nothing.
Fixes: sort the data first, use a branch-free form (a conditional move), or keep branches regular. A 2-bit counter handles a loop well: it mispredicts only once at loop exit.

title: Eight additions in one instruction

steps.say: Add two arrays of 8 floats: c[i] = a[i] + b[i]. a holds 1 to 8, b holds 10 to 80. Each float is 4 bytes, so each array is 32 bytes.
Scalar code: one addss instruction adds one pair. First lane: 1 + 10 = 11.
The scalar loop needs 8 adds (plus 8 loads, 8 stores and loop counting). About 8 instructions of work for 8 results.
Now reset. SIMD means one instruction works on many values. AVX2 has 256-bit registers: 8 floats side by side (8 lanes).
One vaddps adds all 8 lanes at the same time, in about the same time as one scalar add.
AVX-512 has 512-bit registers: 16 floats per instruction, so up to 16 times more work per instruction than scalar code.
Failure case 1: the array has 1,003 floats. The loop does 125 vector steps of 8, then 3 left-over items need a scalar tail or a mask.
Failure case 2: an if inside the loop. All lanes run both sides; a mask decides which results to keep, so you pay for both paths.
Failure case 3: memory limits you. Reading 2 arrays and writing 1 moves 12 bytes per float. At 50 GB/s RAM bandwidth that is about 4 billion floats per second, so 16 lanes can't help a big array.

title: DRAM: row hit, row miss and refresh

steps.say: A DRAM bank is a grid of tiny capacitors. A charged one means 1. Data is read one whole row (8 KB) at a time, never one bit alone.
The CPU wants a byte in row 5000. The row buffer is empty. The controller sends ACTIVATE row 5000.
The row is copied into the row buffer. Reading a row drains the capacitors, so the chip rewrites them. This takes tRCD, about 14 ns.
Now READ column 40. The data comes out after tCAS, about 14 ns more. Total from empty: about 28 ns inside the chip.
Next access is also in row 5000: a row hit. Only tCAS, 14 ns. The controller reorders requests to get more hits.
Now an access to row 7000: a row conflict. The open row must be closed first.
Then ACTIVATE row 7000 and READ. Cost: tRP 14 + tRCD 14 + tCAS 14 = about 42 ns, 3 times a row hit. With controller and bus, the CPU sees about 70 to 90 ns.
Capacitors leak. Every cell must be refreshed every 64 ms. The controller sends a refresh about every 7.8 microseconds.
During a refresh (about 350 ns) the bank can't answer. A request that arrives then waits. This is one source of tail latency.

title: Why an SSD write becomes many writes

steps.say: Flash has a rule: a page can be written only once, and only a whole block (hundreds of pages) can be erased. Here a block has 4 pages. Block 7 is on the left, block 9 is empty on the right.
The host writes logical block 100 (LBA 100). The FTL puts it in the next free page, block 7 page 0, and records the mapping.
The host writes LBA 101, 102 as well. They fill pages 1 and 2.
Now the host overwrites LBA 100. Flash can't change a page in place. The FTL writes the new data to page 3 and marks page 0 as stale (garbage).
Block 7 is full: 1 stale page and 3 valid pages. The drive has to free it to accept more writes.
Garbage collection: copy the 3 valid pages to block 9 first. These are extra writes the host never asked for.
Then erase block 7 as a whole. An erase takes about 3 ms, 6 times slower than a page write.
Count the flash writes: the host wrote 4 pages (L100, 101, 102, L100 again). The flash wrote 4 + 3 copies = 7. Write amplification is 7/4 = 1.75.

Cost: each block survives only about 1,000 to 3,000 erase cycles (TLC). Random small writes on a nearly full drive can reach WA of 5 to 10, so the drive dies sooner and writes slow down. Free space (over-provisioning) keeps WA low.

title: An NMOS transistor as a switch

steps.say: A transistor has a source, a drain and a gate. The silicon under the gate is p-type: it has holes and almost no free electrons, so no current can flow between source and drain.
Gate at 0 V: the switch is OFF. The leakage is only about nanoamps, since the channel is blocked.
Now raise the gate to 0.8 V. This is above the threshold voltage (Vt about 0.3 V). The gate is insulated by a ~1 nm oxide, so no current flows into it, only an electric field.
The positive field pulls electrons from the source toward the surface under the gate, and pushes holes away.
A thin layer of electrons, a few nm thick, forms a channel (n-type inversion layer). The source and drain are now connected: the switch is ON.
The drain is at 0.8 V, so electrons drift from source to drain. The transistor passes about 0.5 mA per micrometre of width, and charges the load.
Speed and energy: charging a 1 fF load to 0.8 V takes about 5 to 10 picoseconds and uses about 0.3 femtojoules (1/2 x C x V squared). A chip does billions of these per second.
Turn the gate back to 0 V: the channel disappears and the switch opens again.

Failure case: as transistors shrink, the oxide is only a few atoms thick. Electrons tunnel through it and leak even when OFF. Leakage is now a big part of chip power, and heat is why clock speeds stopped near 5 GHz.

title: A p-n junction: bias decides if current flows

steps.say: A p-type piece has many mobile holes (h+). An n-type piece has many mobile electrons (e-). Joined into a p-n junction they form a diode.
At the joint, electrons diffuse into the p side and holes diffuse into the n side. They meet and cancel out (recombine).

This leaves fixed charged atoms behind and no mobile carriers: a depletion zone about 0.5 micrometres wide. Its electric field builds a barrier of about 0.7 V in silicon, which stops further diffusion.
Reverse bias: connect the battery so p is negative, 5 V. The field pulls carriers away from the junction and the depletion zone widens.
The barrier is now bigger, so almost no current flows: only a leakage of about 1 nanoamp. The diode is a closed valve.
Forward bias: flip the battery to +0.7 V. The external voltage cancels the built-in barrier and the depletion zone shrinks.
Holes and electrons are pushed into the junction and cross it. Current grows exponentially: each extra 60 mV makes it about 10 times larger. At 0.7 V it can be several mA.
This one-way behaviour makes rectifiers and LEDs. It is also the building block of the transistor: an NMOS has two p-n junctions around its channel.
Failure case: reverse voltage too high (for example 50 V on a 5 V diode). Carriers gain enough energy to knock out more carriers (avalanche breakdown). Current explodes and the diode can burn out.
